sense: for emphasis: I do like it; do come in

terms.grammar: adverb, usually after the first word
evidence: Ter. Ph. 1053–1054: Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō.
Cic. Fam. 14.4.1: ego vērō tē quam prīmum, mea vīta, cupiō vidēre
terms.comment: English stresses the auxiliary; Latin stresses the statement, with vērō or by repeating the verb (Dormiō, “I am asleep”). Facere can stand for a verb just used, as “do” does (Lewis & Short; et ego fēcī, “so did I”); but a short answer repeats the verb itself (see yes).

terms.gloss: I for my part, I really
terms.grammar: adverb, mostly with the first person
evidence: Ter. Eun. 378: Tibi equidem dīcō, manē.
Plaut. Most. 332–333c: nōlō equidem tē adflīgī

terms.grammar: interrogative adverb with the present indicative
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 1387: quid stās? quīn intrō īs?
Plaut. Asin. 597: quīn tū hīc manēs?
terms.comment: The urging “do”: “do go in”, “do stay”. Lewis & Short: only in exhortation or remonstrance, never asking for a fact.

terms.register: in this sense, vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.
terms.comment: Granting what was asked: “do go, then” (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō. — Eāmus intrō hinc. — Fīat.
phrases.english: Invite me to dinner. — I do invite you! — Let’s go in. — Very well.

phrases.latin: ego vērō tē quam prīmum, mea vīta, cupiō vidēre
phrases.english: I do want to see you as soon as I can, my darling

phrases.latin: Quid, taceam? quīn tū īs dormītum? — Dormiō, nē occlāmitēs.
phrases.english: What, me be quiet? Why don’t you go to bed? — I am asleep: stop shouting.
Why are you standing there? Do go in.

phrases.latin: Ī sānē, et quantum potest parāta fac sint omnia.
phrases.english: Do go, and get everything ready as fast as you can.

phrases.latin: et ego fēcī quī litterās Graecās senex didicī
phrases.english: and so did I, who learnt Greek as an old man
